analysis.one_liner: Creates personal investment accounts within Social Security for younger workers, with a guaranteed minimum benefit, funded partly by raising the retirement age.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 13, 2008, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed Social Security for people born after 1962: instead of all payroll taxes going into the traditional program, 4% of each worker's wages would go into a personal investment account managed like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, with low fees and a guaranteed monthly benefit at least equal to today's formula. To pay for it, the bill also raised the full retirement age to 68 for future retirees, deepened the benefit reduction for retiring early, and required general tax dollars to top up the trust funds when needed. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born in 1963 or later would have gained personal retirement accounts they own outright, with the guarantee that total benefits never fall below the current formula and a higher minimum benefit for the poorest retirees. Any leftover account balance could be kept or left to family.

how_it_helps.text: It would divert 4% of each covered worker's wages into a personal 'SAFE account' managed like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, which the worker owns outright, with an annual administrative fee capped at 0.57%.

It guarantees a total monthly benefit no lower than the current Social Security benefit, and sets a minimum monthly benefit of 135% of the poverty line for new retirees starting in 2025, which would raise benefits for the lowest earners.

At retirement, enough of the account is converted into a federal annuity to cover the guaranteed benefit, leftover funds cover survivor benefits, and anything beyond that is the worker's to keep or pass on—money that under current law would never be the worker's property.

analysis.who_pays: Future retirees would bear the cost: a higher full retirement age (68), larger penalties for retiring early, and traditional benefits reduced by the amount moved into investment accounts. General taxpayers would also fund required annual top-ups to keep the trust funds solvent.

drawbacks.text: It raised the full retirement age to 68 for people reaching early retirement age after 2024 and made early-retirement benefit reductions larger, meaning many workers would have to work longer or accept smaller monthly checks.

It cut the traditional Social Security benefit for participants by the amount diverted into their investment accounts, so retirement income would depend partly on stock market results during a worker's lifetime.
It required annual general-tax appropriations to keep the trust funds at full balance, effectively shifting part of the program's cost onto general federal revenue and adding to budget pressure.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no base of support even before it reached a committee that took no action on it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered an appealing idea—personal retirement accounts with a guaranteed minimum benefit—but its trade-off was real: workers would give up part of their traditional benefit and many would work a year longer, while the government took on a permanent obligation to top up the trust funds. It was never debated in committee, so its design was never tested or improved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Hagel introduced the bill on March 13, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The committee held no hearings, marked up no version of the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor; it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: no one gained a new benefit, and the traditional Social Security structure—with no personal accounts and no change to the retirement age—remained untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the Social Security status quo

for.name: Sen. Chuck Hagel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its investment-account plan for Social Security.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes, the bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan pattern.

industries.note: The bill itself routed accounts through a government fund modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan with a fee cap, so it did not directly hand accounts to Wall Street, but it required a study of using private annuities for distributions and would have grown the pool of invested retirement assets. Its failure left the industry's role unchanged.

industries.industry: Current Social Security beneficiaries and the program itself
industries.note: A major bill reshaping Social Security's financing, retirement age, and benefit formulas never got a committee hearing or vote, leaving the program's long-term financing question unaddressed that Congress.
